animals.blurb: Infamous for their venomous bite and the red hourglass marking on females. Despite their reputation, bites are rarely fatal and they are not aggressive—preferring to flee or play dead.
animals.hint: A shiny black spider with a red hourglass warning

animals.blurb: Known for the violin-shaped marking on their back. Their venom can cause tissue damage, but they bite only when trapped against skin. True recluses, they avoid humans.
animals.hint: A reclusive spider with a violin-shaped marking

animals.blurb: Large, striking orb weavers with distinctive zigzag web decorations called stabilimenta. Despite their size, they are harmless to humans and beneficial predators of garden pests.
animals.hint: A large zigzag web weaver in black and yellow

animals.blurb: Fuzzy, curious spiders with excellent vision from large front-facing eyes. They don't build webs but actively hunt prey, leaping many times their body length. They often seem to watch you back.
animals.hint: A fuzzy curious spider that leaps and watches you

animals.blurb: Large, fast-running hunters that don't build webs. Females carry their egg sacs attached to their spinnerets, then carry hatched spiderlings on their backs for days.
animals.hint: A furry hunter that carries babies on her back

animals.blurb: Large, docile spiders often seen crossing roads in fall as males search for mates. Despite their size, their venom is mild and they prefer to flee rather than bite.
animals.hint: A gentle giant crossing desert roads in autumn

animals.blurb: Not actually spiders but harvestmen—they have one body segment and no venom glands. Despite the myth, they cannot bite humans. Their long legs detach to distract predators.
animals.hint: A long-legged myth—no venom, can't bite

animals.blurb: The most venomous scorpion in North America, capable of climbing walls and hiding in shoes. Their sting is painful and can be dangerous to children and elderly, but rarely fatal.
animals.hint: A wall-climbing scorpion with a painful sting

animals.blurb: The most common scorpion in the US, identified by two dark stripes on its back. Their sting is painful but not dangerous to healthy adults. They glow bright blue under UV light.
animals.hint: A striped scorpion that glows under blacklight

animals.blurb: Named for the white spot on females' backs, these aggressive ticks are expanding northward. Their bites can cause a rare allergy to red meat called alpha-gal syndrome.
animals.hint: A tick that can make you allergic to red meat
